title: Mitigating Label Shift in Tabular In-Context Learning via Test-Time Posterior Adjustment
claim: Standard in-context predictors collapse toward the majority training class; a simple test-time probability rescaling corrects this bias.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, zoom-in callout with bar charts showing before/after
description: Two framed panels side by side. Panel (a), titled TabPFN, shows a grey Transformer box. Below it are context examples (red and blue dots in a red-outlined box) and unlabeled test cells with question marks (blue-outlined box). Black arrows run upward into predicted dots, nearly all red. A pink callout reads "Biased toward the majority class". Panel (b), + DistPFN, repeats the same Transformer and inputs. It adds a row of "before adjustment" predictions, green arrows, and an "after adjustment" row in which some red dots flip to blue. A dashed green zoom callout on the right compares bar charts. The pink before-chart is 0.55 red and 0.45 blue. A big green arrow leads to the yellow after-chart at 0.40 red and 0.60 blue. It is labeled "Test-time Adaptation: Distribution Adjustment". Red and blue dots mark the classes, and green marks the proposed fix.
caption: Overall framework of DistPFN. (a) TabPFN exhibits a majority-class bias under label shift, predicting test instances toward the majority class in the training dataset. (b) DistPFN mitigates this bias via a simple test-time adaptation method that rescales the predicted class probabilities for each test instance.
abstract: TabPFN has recently gained attention as a foundation model for tabular datasets, achieving strong performance by leveraging in-context learning on synthetic data. However, we find that TabPFN is vulnerable to label shift, often overfitting to the majority class in the training dataset. To address this limitation, we propose DistPFN, the first test-time posterior adjustment method designed for tabular foundation models. DistPFN rescales predicted class probabilities by downweighting the influence of the training prior (i.e., the class distribution of the context) and emphasizing the contribution of the model's predicted posterior, without architectural modification or additional training. We further introduce DistPFN-T, which incorporates temperature scaling to adaptively control the adjustment strength based on the discrepancy between prior and posterior. We evaluate our methods on over 250 OpenML datasets, demonstrating substantial improvements for various TabPFN-based models in classification tasks under label shift, while maintaining strong performance in standard settings without label shift. Code is available at this repository: https://github.com/seunghan96/DistPFN.
